text.content:
The Gull's Job — GM Overview

An optional sidequest for Days 12–15 in Gradsul, after @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GradJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GrPgShip000]{The Kestrel Wife} and before @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GradJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GrPgSail000]{Out of the Sheldomar}. GM only. It costs the party no days: the Kestrel Wife does not sail until Day 15 whatever they do.

The shape of it

  1. Day 12, night — @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgBrawl00]{The Brawl at the Mermaid}. The party is drinking at the Mermaid's Inn when the Weigher's men try to carry off a young noblewoman in a grey veil. Nobody draws steel under the mermaid. The party saves her.
  2. Day 12, late — @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgReveal0]{The Walk Home}. They see her home. In a dark lane the second half of the snatch team is waiting, and the rooftops drop on it — her people. The fair maiden lifts her veil and gives orders. She is the Gull, and she has a job for strangers.
  3. Days 13–14 — @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgPrep000]{Laying the Job}. Case the Royal Museum. Get the Pearl measured for the forger. Find a way past a Sea Mage's ward. Notice, or don't, that the chandler who sold them their tools is selling them in turn.
  4. Night of Day 14 — @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgNight00]{The Night}. Swap the Mooncurser's Pearl for Pike's copy, in @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-scenes.Scene.BR2T1ScnMuse0000]{Gradsul — The Royal Museum}, without anyone knowing it happened. Heist, not battle: every fight in that building makes the morning worse.
  5. Before dawn, Day 15 — @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgPay0000]{Payoff & Consequences}. The Pearl into the Gull's hand; clean papers into the party's. Up the plank on the morning tide.

The truth

@UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActGull0000]{Lady Ysolde Dunmore — the Gull} is twenty-four, the last of an attainted noble house, and the head of the Docklands guild, the Mooncursers. Twelve years ago her father, Lord Harlan Dunmore, was beheaded at the River Gate for the Dunmore Lights — twenty years of false lamps on Dunmore Head and the wrecks they made — and the Crown took everything his house owned. One of the things it took was the Mooncurser's Pearl: a black pearl the size of a pigeon's egg, set in a tarnished silver gull's foot, which by the oldest custom on the waterfront seats whoever brings it at the head of the Low Table, where the crews settle what the Watch would settle worse. It is not magic. It is worse: it is custom. It has been in a glass case in the Royal Museum ever since, under a little card in the Keeper's hand that calls it a token of the Dunmore wreckers.

The Gull has ruled the Docklands for seven years by wit, money and fear, without the Pearl. @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActWeigh000]{Hobb Garrow — the Weigher}, master of the Orgsworth crews, means to take it, call the Low Table, and sit at its head with the Docklands in his pocket. He has just learned who the Gull is, because @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActBreck000]{Widow Annis Breck} sold him her face. So on Day 12 he tries to have her carried off from the one room in Gradsul where nobody draws a blade — and the party is in the room.

The Gull needs the Pearl back before the Weigher lifts it, and she needs strangers to do it, for two reasons she will give them and one she will not. The two: the Weigher has a man watching the museum who knows every Mooncurser face, and by the old custom the Pearl must be lifted from wherever it lies by a hand sworn to no crew — the sea gives it; nobody takes it — and only then does whoever brings it to the Low Table sit at its head. The third: if a Mooncurser is caught in a royal museum, it is war on the waterfront, and the waterfront is wool and tar and timber and it burns.

What the party gets

Clean papers into Hardby, made by @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActPike0000]{Absalom Pike}, exactly as promised, and nothing else:

  • A provenance docket from a real Gradsul wool-house that owes the Gull, recording that the delegation's samples were damaged on the road and replaced at Gradsul under the house's seal. It matters only if the samples were lost at the Ford (@UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1FordJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1FdPgTerr000]{Terrain, the Cart Clock & Outcomes}): it closes that first crack in the cover, because the letters and the bales now agree on paper.
  • A weigh-ticket for their bales, forged by Pike in a weigh-house clerk's hand, marked weighed short, with a gold lion folded inside it. That is not a Gull arrangement but an old custom of every tide-waiter on the Azure coast: a ticket that says weighed short with a coin in it means count the bales, take the coin, write nothing, and the boy who boards at the Hardby mole knows it as well as anyone. Nobody in Hardby learns whose ticket it was. That cancels the one line @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1QRefJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1QrPgHandoff]{Hand-off to Phase 3} adds when the hull track reached segment 2 — the harbour takes you in without a flicker, as @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3ArrivalJrnl.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3ArPgArr02Cmm]{Arrival — Commercial Cover} says it should.

Both push Phase 3 back toward its own canon; neither adds anything to it. Put a note on the back of the hand-off sheet: Gull's papers — docket (y/n), weigh-ticket (y/n).

What must not change

  • Nothing learned in Gradsul reaches the firm. The Gull does not know there is a firm, and nothing in this journal tells her. She never asks the party's business; she knows only what everyone on her docks knows — the hull, its destination, five women from the west. Under no outcome, including a double-cross, does she sell them to anybody: she settles her own accounts.
  • The circular is untouched. @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1FordJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1FdPgTally00]{The Visibility Tally} is a count of the Ford and nothing else; nothing done in Gradsul changes the line you put in the letter.
  • The Kestrel Wife sails on Day 15. The worst outcome here moves her from the morning tide to the evening tide of the same day. The calendar does not move.
  • Roke stays Roke. He hears about this only if the Harbour Warden holds his tide or somebody throws fire in the Mermaid's, and either way he says one sentence and treats the party exactly as before.
  • Per-PC threads are untouched. The spotlight notes on these pages are table advice, not beats.

XP

AwardParty XPEach (five PCs)
The brawl: Dogger and four toughs850170
The job, as a milestone — Clean1,500300
The job, as a milestone — any other success1,000200
Fights in the museum, the chase, anything else—nothing extra

Never more than 640 each in Gradsul. @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1QRefJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1QrPgXP00000]{XP and the Sixth-Level Line} lands the party on 13,359 at most after the Grey Fee, with the boarding's second wave, and sixth level is 14,000: anything above 640 here levels them before Day 37, on the wrong deck. The most this page can award is 470, so the party still makes sixth in Woolly Bay, and any Gradsul award at all now carries them over the line there even if you run neither dial.

Hooks into the Mermaid's

Any one: Wick Ferrin, carrying their bales up the plank, tells them that if they are ashore tonight they want the Mermaid's, because there's a mermaid, a real one; Vole, walking them to the water, says the same; or it is simply the loudest door between the Kestrel Wife's quay and the wool-house where they are sleeping. If they never go in, there is no job, and Gradsul is colour.

Pieces

  • Scenes: @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-scenes.Scene.BR2T1ScnGrad0000]{Gradsul — City Map (GM)} (the gold pins are this job), @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-scenes.Scene.BR2T1ScnMuse0000]{Gradsul — The Royal Museum}, and @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-scenes.Scene.BR2T1ScnMerm0000]{Gradsul — The Mermaid's Inn} with @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-scenes.Scene.BR2T1ScnMermUp00]{The Mermaid's Inn, Upstairs}. The last two are drawn on your own copy of 2-Minute Tabletop's The Mermaid Inn, which the module does not ship: see The Brawl at the Mermaid for where the files go.
  • Sheets: Gradsul folder in First Travel Intermission — NPCs. Cast list: @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GPplJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1PpPgUnder00]{Who's Who — The Underworld}.
  • Places: @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GzetJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GzPgUnder00]{The Waterfront Underneath} and @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GzetJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GzPgInst000]{the Royal Museum entry}.
  • Handouts: @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgHandout]{Pike's Papers} (with the docket) or @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgTicket0]{The Weigh-Ticket} (without it), both safe to show.

The Mermaid's Inn

Day 12, after dark. Read as the party comes in through the double doors. About two minutes.

Read aloud

You hear the Mermaid's before you see it: a roar of voices out of a pair of wide double doors at the end of a Docklands lane, and over the doors, on a beam black with age, five words in white paint, each letter as tall as a hand: NO STEEL UNDER THE MERMAID.

Inside, the room is enormous — it was a warehouse once, and the beams are ship's timbers — and it is full. Sailors, stevedores, fishwives, clerks, two cadets in blue coats trying to look as though they come here often. Long tables, a bar along one side the length of a ship, and lanterns everywhere. But nobody is looking at the lanterns.

In the middle of the room stands a tank. A great box of thick green glass in a bronze frame, taller than a man, wider than a cart, full of water to the brim and lit from somewhere underneath, so that the whole room swims in moving blue light. And in the tank, there is a woman. Her hair floats around her like smoke. Below the waist she is a long silver-grey fish's tail, and she turns in the water as slowly as a leaf falling, and every time she turns, the light turns with her and slides across every face in the room.

The noise does not stop, exactly. It just gets softer every time she comes round.

A very large woman with cropped grey hair and a belaying pin through her apron string looks you over from behind the bar, reaches the same conclusion about all five of you, and points at the only empty table — at the far end under the stair, beside a curtained booth where a young woman in grey, a veil over her hair, sits with a thin man in black who is writing.

“Sit there,” says the very large woman. “Drink what you like. Keep your irons where they are. Welcome to the Mermaid's.”

After the read-aloud

That is @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActGannet00]{Maud Gannet}. The mer is @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActOona0000]{Oona}. The lady in grey is the Gull, and the thin man is Pike, taking her commission for the replica; the party will not hear a word of it. Give them a few minutes of the room — the beer is good and cheap, the regulars want to know where they are from, and @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActFerrand0]{Josca Ferrand} is at the bar being recognised — then start @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgBrawl00]{the brawl}.

The Brawl at the Mermaid

Day 12, night. A rescue, not a hit-point race: the question is whether the Weigher's men get one woman out of the front doors. 850 XP.

The room

@UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-scenes.Scene.BR2T1ScnMerm0000]{Gradsul — The Mermaid's Inn}, with @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-scenes.Scene.BR2T1ScnMermUp00]{The Mermaid's Inn, Upstairs} for the gallery. Five-foot squares.

  • The front doors — wide double doors in the south wall, left of centre, opening on the lane where the Weigher's cart is waiting.
  • The booths — three curtained booths along the west wall, on a raised boardwalk. The Gull and Pike are in the north booth, under the west stair; the party's table is the nearest one on the floor.
  • The floor — flagstones and a dozen round tables, thirty regulars. Difficult terrain once the chairs go over.
  • The tank — on the floor, west of the middle. Total cover. Thick green glass that has survived worse than anything that happens tonight (see Brawl rules).
  • The bar — the long counter across the east end, with Maud behind it, the crossbow under it, and the back door to the yard in the east wall behind it.
  • The stairs and the gallery — a stair at each end of the north wall up to a gallery that runs round an open well over the middle of the floor, with rooms to let at either end.

The map files. Both scenes point at blooming-rot-2-local/mermaid-inn/MermaidInnFloor1.png and MermaidInnFloor2.png in your Foundry Data folder. If a scene comes up blank, unzip those two files from your MermaidInn.zip into that folder on whichever machine runs your world. The walls, doors, curtains and pins are already traced to them, on the map's own 140-pixel grid.

The snatch

@UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActDogger00]{Dogger Haines} and four @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActWTough00]{Weigher's Toughs}, all with saps, none with steel. It runs like this:

  1. The decoy. Dogger starts a fight at the far end of the floor — a table thrown, a man punched, a lot of shouting — and Maud's two potboys go to stop it.
  2. The grab. Two toughs come out of the crowd at the back, one each side of the Gull, and grapple her; a third throws a flour sack over her head. The fourth and Dogger (who has worked his way back) cover them.
  3. The door. They need three rounds to get her from the booth along the boardwalk and across the floor to the front doors, because a struggling woman is heavy — and she has gone limp, which makes her heavier. Carrying her moves them at half speed, and both carriers must keep their grapple.

She picks the party. In the half-second before the toughs reach her, the lady in grey grabs the arm of the nearest PC — “Please —” — and puts that PC between herself and them. She chose them because they were the only people in the room sworn to nobody; the party will not find that out until later. Insight DC 15, any time in the fight: she went limp at exactly the right moment, the way a sailor goes limp in the water.

If the party does nothing at all, the regulars do it for them, slowly, and the toughs get her out on round three. Go to If she is taken.

Read aloud — the snatch

Read when you start it, a few minutes after they sit down. About forty-five seconds. It ends on the grab; roll initiative on the last word.

It starts at the other end of the room, down by the front doors: a bench goes over, a man goes over the bench, and somebody's tankard hits the bronze frame of the tank with a sound like a bell. Half the room turns to look. Two potboys go over the bar like hounds over a gate.

In the tank, the mer turns once, sharply, and is gone downward in a flash of silver, and the blue light shakes on every wall.

Nobody is looking at the booth beside your table. Two big men in porters' smocks have come out of the crowd, one at each end of it, unhurried, and a third behind them has a flour sack in his hands.

The young woman in grey sees them half a second before they reach her. Her hand closes hard on the arm of whichever of you is nearest.

“Please —”

Brawl rules

  • Everyone knocks out. In the Mermaid's, every melee attack that would drop a creature to 0 hit points leaves it at 1 hit point and Unconscious instead, as the knocking-out rule allows, unless the attacker says otherwise out loud — and then the room turns on them.
  • Improvised weapons are everywhere. Bench, chair, stool, tankard, bottle, a leg of mutton: 1d4 bludgeoning, or 1d6 for something big held in two hands. A bottle breaks on a hit and becomes a 1d4 slashing weapon, which counts as steel.
  • Grapple, shove and trip are encouraged. A creature shoved into the tank takes 1d4 bludgeoning and the glass does not care. Breaking it needs a deliberate effort (AC 13, 40 hit points of glass): then the room is knee-deep in harbour water (difficult terrain), Oona is gone, and Maud's bill is two hundred gold.
  • Oona dives into the sea channel the moment the first table goes over. The tank stays lit.
  • The gallery rail. A creature shoved or thrown off the gallery falls 10 feet onto the floor, or onto a table: 1d6 bludgeoning, prone, and the room cheers.
  • Elle's room. A halfling monk in a fist-fight with no blades allowed is the best thing that will happen to this table all week. Let her have it.

Steel, and what counts

At the end of each round, every creature holding a drawn blade or a nocked bow — or wearing visible spell effects, or having cast a spell anyone can see, this round — is set upon by the regulars: DC 13 Strength or Dexterity saving throw (its choice) or grappled (escape DC 13) and disarmed, and the crowd keeps trying every round until the steel is down. Dropping it ends it at once.

  • Counts: any blade, including a bottle broken into one; Alicia's pact blade, however it arrives — a sword out of thin air is still a sword, and the regulars have opinions; drawn bows; visible spells (lightning, fire, radiance, anything with a light or a sound or an effect a drunk can point at).
  • Does not count: fists, feet, furniture, a staff or a club or a druid's shillelagh (it is wood, and Maud is a stickler for the letter), and any spell nobody can see working.
  • Fire is worse than steel. Anyone who throws fire in a room full of tar-soaked sailors and timber is grappled by everybody, barred from the Mermaid's for life, and the story is on the Kestrel Wife's deck before breakfast: Roke heard about it, and his look rests on her (@UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1BriefJrnl00.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1BrPgCal0000]{Party Calibration & the Fire Rule}).

Round three: one of the toughs panics and pulls a knife. Show the table what happens to him. That is the rule, demonstrated, and the toughs know it.

Round three, when the tough pulls his knife.

Somewhere in the scrum a blade comes out — a short sailor's knife, nothing much — and the whole room makes the same sound at once, a sort of growl. Thirty people who were fighting each other a moment ago stop, and turn, and go for the man with the knife. He disappears under them. When the crowd steps back he is sitting against the bar with his nose broken and no knife, and Maud Gannet is standing over him with her belaying pin, not even breathing hard.

“Not under the mermaid,” she says, to the whole room.

The rest of the room

  • Maud lets it run one round for the entertainment, then wades in with the belaying pin and her potboys. If anyone drew steel she clears them first; if nobody did, she clears the Weigher's men, because she knows whose men they are.
  • Josca Ferrand joins on round two, barehanded, on whichever side looks outnumbered, laughing.
  • Pike spends the whole fight under the booth table with his satchel clutched to his chest. If someone helps him out, he thanks them three times and does not give his name.
  • Nye is outside the front doors with the lantern. The cart men knock him down in the lane.

Outcomes

  • They stop the snatch. The toughs break when two are down or Maud reaches them. Dogger goes to the Watch, slung over Maud's shoulder, and is back on the street by noon on Day 13: the Weigher pays Captain Pritchard too. The lady in grey, shaking, asks the party to see her home: go to @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgReveal0]{The Walk Home}.
  • If she is taken, the cart gets twenty yards down the lane before the rooftops fall on it (the same Mooncursers as the walk home). The party, following, arrives to find the carters groaning on the cobbles and the lady in grey standing over them, sack in her hand, giving orders. Skip to the reveal.
  • If the party kept the rule, Maud gives them the freedom of the Mermaid's for as long as they are in Gradsul. If they broke it, they are barred, and Maud tells them so with real regret.

The Walk Home & the Offer

Day 12, late. The escort, the second team, the veil, and the job.

The walk

She gives her name as Ysolde and her direction as a cousin's house on the Promenade, and very little else; her elderly coachman, @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActNye00000]{Gethin Nye}, bleeding from a cut scalp, lights the way. The way to the Promenade from the Mermaid's runs up through the Docklands by Tarpot Lane, narrow, steep and unlit, under the eaves of the net-lofts.

If they will not walk her home, Nye finds them at their wool-house in the morning with her thanks and an invitation, and the net loft and the offer happen on Day 13 instead; skip the lane.

Read aloud — Tarpot Lane

Read as they climb Tarpot Lane with her. About forty-five seconds. It ends with five men in the lane; let the party draw before the next one.

Tarpot Lane climbs away from the water so steeply that it is half steps, under the overhanging eaves of the net-lofts, where the air smells of tar and old rope and the cobbles are slick with something you would rather not name. There are no lamps. There is only the coachman's lantern swinging ahead of you, and the sound of the harbour falling away below.

The lady in grey walks with her veil down and says almost nothing. Once she thanks you again, very quietly, as though she were afraid of being overheard.

Halfway up, the lantern stops.

Three men step out of a doorway ahead. Behind you, two more come out of an alley, and stand, and wait. One of them is dabbing at a split lip. They have come from the Mermaid's, and they are not carrying saps any more.

The read-aloud ends with five men in the lane: the cart crew and the rest of the Weigher's snatch team, who have heard how the inn went and mean to finish it. Let the party draw — out here there is no mermaid — and then, before anybody can swing, read the next part.

Read aloud — off the roofs

Read before anybody swings. About a minute.

Something comes down off the roof.

Then several somethings: shapes in tarred jackets dropping out of the eaves on both sides of the lane, silent, quick, landing on the men in front and the men behind. It is over in about the time it takes to draw breath. Five men are on the cobbles. Six people you have never seen are standing over them, breathing hard, with knives they are already putting away.

And all of them — the coachman too — have turned, and are looking past you, at the girl in grey. Waiting.

She lifts her veil back over her hair. It is the same pale, gentle, frightened face. It is not frightened any more.

“Put them in the river at Pitch Stair,” she says, “and see that they can swim first. Then tell Garrow I'm home.” The voice is the same voice. Everything else about it has changed.

Then she turns back to you, and for a moment the girl from the inn is back, and she means it. “Thank you. That was real, all of it, and you didn't have to. Most people in that room had a reason not to.”

The girl goes away again. “My name is Ysolde Dunmore, and on the Promenade that is all I am. Down here they call me the Gull.” She tilts her head toward the dark end of the lane, where the river is. “You've made an enemy of the Weigher tonight. Walk with me, and I'll tell you what he weighs.”

The net loft

Read as they climb into the loft.

The net loft hangs out over the river on old black piles, and the way up is a ladder. Inside it is all tarred rope and lamplight: nets hung from every beam like grey curtains, a stove ticking in the corner, and a long table under the lamps with a chart of the harbour weighted flat at its corners with a knife, a lead sounding-weight, a teacup and a gull's skull. Two or three people in tarred jackets look up as you come in, find reasons to be somewhere else, and go.

The coachman lowers himself onto a bench with a grunt and lets somebody see to his head.

The lady in grey takes the chair at the head of the table as though it had always been hers, and pours your wine herself.

She takes them to a net loft over the water, all tarred rope and lamplight and a long table with a chart on it, where a handful of Mooncursers find reasons to be elsewhere. Wine, bread, dry cloths, a bowl of water for Nye's head. Then she tells them, plainly, most of The truth from the overview page: her father, the Lights, the Pearl, the Low Table, the Weigher, and the job.

The offer

She says it plainly, once, and then answers questions.

“I want the Pearl out of that case and into my hand before the Low Table sits, which is at the turn of the morning tide on the day your hull sails. I want a copy left in its place, so good that the Keeper never knows. Nobody hurt — not his wardens, not him, nobody. Do that, and you go up the Kestrel Wife's plank with clean papers for Hardby, and nobody in that harbour writes down a word about you.”

Her answers

If they askShe says
Why us?“You're sworn to nobody, you leave on the morning tide, and I've just watched you fight in a room where nobody's allowed to win properly.”
Why not do it yourself?The watcher on the museum corner knows every Mooncurser face; and by the custom, the Pearl has to be lifted by a hand sworn to no crew before anybody may carry it to the Low Table. “The sea gives it. Nobody takes it.” She will not say the third reason unless an Insight DC 15 finds it: a Mooncurser caught in a royal museum is a war, and wars on this waterfront burn.
Is it magic?“No. It's worse. It's custom.”
What's in it for us?The papers (see the overview), described exactly. She will not pay in coin; she says coin is how people get caught.
What if we say no?“Then you've done me a kindness and I owe you one, and you'll sail with my thanks.” She means it. Nothing follows them aboard.
Who sold you?“Somebody I'll find. That isn't your concern.” It becomes their concern on Day 13.
Why should we trust you?“Because you know who I am. You could count the people who do on your hands, and one of them sold me tonight. That's a better bond than coin.”
What we want in HardbyShe does not ask, and will not. “I don't want to know your business. I want the Pearl.”

Spotlight

Whoever does the talking for the party is negotiating with someone better at it than they are, and the Gull enjoys that. Let her concede one thing, gracefully, to whoever pushes hardest: a Mooncurser boat at the river stair under the castle hill on the night; a Mooncurser on the roof opposite the museum, who whistles once if a patrol turns into the street (one round's warning); or Nye and the coach waiting in the lane behind the yard.

What she gives them tonight

  • A name and a door: Widow Breck's chandlery on Tarpot Lane, for tools and a builder's plan of the museum, on the Gull's account.
  • A name and a time: Pike, at the Nautical Library, who needs the Pearl's measure by dusk on Day 13.
  • A deadline: the net loft, before dawn on Day 15.
  • A question: whether their samples came through the road. If they tell her the samples were lost — or if Vole has already told the market — Pike makes the docket.

Laying the Job

Day 13 and Day 14. Four legs, in any order, and one leak. The party does not have to do all of them; each one they skip makes the night harder.

1. Case the museum

Read on their first afternoon visit. About a minute. It shows them nothing the table below does not already give for free.

The Royal Museum is a narrow townhouse in Havverd squeezed between two grander neighbours, with a brass plate by the door and, just inside it, a donation box on a post, watched over from behind a desk by a white-haired gentleman with the attention of a cat at a mousehole. He is the Keeper, and he is delighted to see you. He is delighted to see anybody.

The ground floor is wreckage, lovingly arranged: two great anchors, a ship's bell on its frame, a wheel, coils of old cable, and on trestles in the middle of the room a crowned figurehead three times the size of a woman, staring at the ceiling with an expression of mild surprise.

Upstairs is the gallery: one long room with tall windows on the street, ship models under glass down both sides and charts on every wall. At the far end, up two shallow steps under a skylight, is an alcove with a single domed case in it, on its own. In the case, on faded velvet, lies a black pearl the size of a pigeon's egg, held in a tarnished silver claw shaped like a gull's foot.

The little card beside it reads, in a careful hand: A token of the Dunmore wreckers.

The Royal Museum is open to anyone with a copper sparrow in the afternoons, and @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActWhitlk00]{Keeper Ambrose Whitlock} is delighted to show visitors round. A visit gives them the building as drawn on @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-scenes.Scene.BR2T1ScnMuse0000]{Gradsul — The Royal Museum}. Checks, for anyone who looks:

CheckWhat they learn
AnyoneTwo floors open to the public; the Pearl in a glass-domed case alone in the raised alcove at the back of the gallery, under a skylight; two old night wardens come on at dusk; the front doors are barred from inside at night.
Perception DC 12A small iron coal-chute hatch low in the street wall beside the front doors. A second skylight over the stair head.
Investigation DC 13The domed case's lock is a good one (thieves' tools DC 15). The Keeper wears a brass disc on a chain and touches it when he passes the gallery arch.
Arcana DC 13, or detect magicThe whole gallery and its alcove are warded — abjuration, Sea-Mage work. The stair head and the workroom are not.
Ask the Keeper (no check)Ask him about the brass disc and he tells them, proudly, that the gallery has a Sea-Mage's ward and the disc lets him through it; the wardens share one, which lives on a nail, and Sea-Mage Lusk keeps the third. He would never imagine that is information.
Perception DC 14, outsideA one-legged beggar on the corner opposite who is not begging, and who looks hard at every face that goes in. He is the Weigher's watcher. He has never seen any of the party before.

Whitlock will also mention, to anyone who admires the Pearl, that he lectures on the evening of Day 14 at the Royal Explorers' Chapterhouse, on the Dunmore Lights.

2. Pike and the Pearl

Read when they find Pike at the Nautical Library, any time on Day 13.

The Nautical Library is a round stone building in Gartten under a green copper dome, and its reading room is very quiet: a ring of tall desks beneath the dome, a copyist bent over a chart at each, and the scratch of pens like mice in a wall.

The thin man in black from the Mermaid's has the desk furthest from the door. He looks up, knows you, goes white and then pink, and with enormous care puts down his pen.

“Not here,” he whispers. “Please. They think I'm a copyist.” He glances at the window. “I am a copyist.” And then, lower still, with an eagerness he plainly cannot help: “Did she send you about the Pearl? I need its measure by dusk.”

@UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActPike0000]{Absalom Pike} needs the Pearl's true size and a close look at its setting by dusk on Day 13, or the replica will not be finished by dusk on Day 14. The museum is open in the afternoons, so this is a Day 13 visit. Any of:

  • A careful sketch made at the case during a visit: Sleight of Hand or calligrapher's/painter's tools DC 12, done under the Keeper's nose.
  • The Keeper's own catalogue, volume two, which has the Pearl drawn at actual size: talk him into showing it (Persuasion DC 13; DC 10 if somebody has asked him a second question about anything).
  • Pike himself, smuggled in as one of the party's visitors: he is unknown to the watcher and terrified, and he will want to touch the glass.

If they fail or are late, Pike makes it from the Gull's memory and a twelve-year-old drawing: good enough for a night, not for a week. The outcome can be no better than Noticed.

3. The ward

The gallery is warded (rules on @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgMuse000]{The Royal Museum}). Ways past it, from best to worst:

  • The wardens' token, on its nail by the wardens' door, a yard from Sully's elbow. Hab takes it down for every round and hangs it back up, so there is a twenty-minute window between rounds; lifting it means getting past Sully (Sleight of Hand against his passive Perception 15, or a reason for him to leave the room), and it must be back on the nail before Hab's next round. If Hab finds the nail empty, he and Sully each assume the other has it for about a minute, then Sully pulls the rope: Heat 5. Put back in time, nobody ever knows.
  • The Keeper's token, at his lecture on the evening of Day 14 — the Royal Explorers' Chapterhouse, a silver hawk at the door, a hundred people, wine after, done by ten bells, which leaves the night for the job. Sleight of Hand DC 15 to lift it off its chain, DC 12 if somebody is keeping him talking about the Dunmore Lights, which he will do for an hour. He misses it on the morning of Day 15, as the Kestrel Wife is sailing: unless it is back on his chain by then (the Gull's people can manage that, once), the outcome is Noticed at best.
  • Never enter it. A mage hand is not a creature, and nor is a line and a hook. (The hand still has to be conjured somewhere its caster can see.) Anything that can get the case open and the Pearl out from the stair head without a creature crossing the arch is legitimate. Reward it.
  • Dispel it. Quiet tonight; Lusk feels it go out and comes to look in the morning. Noticed at best.

Read aloud — Whitlock's lecture

Evening of Day 14, if they go after the Keeper's token at his lecture.

The Royal Explorers' Chapterhouse is full: a hundred people on benches under painted maps of places nobody in the room has been, beneath the Society's banner, a gold lion within a compass rose on a field of green. The doorman takes a silver hawk from each of you. There is wine at the back for afterwards.

Keeper Whitlock lectures from a lectern, without notes and with enormous pleasure. His subject is the Dunmore Lights: twenty years of false lamps on Dunmore Head, the wrecks they made, the night the Duke's marines went up the cliff path, and the morning at the River Gate. He tells it well. The room shivers in the right places.

When he comes to the Pearl, his hand goes to his chest, where something hangs on a chain under his waistcoat, and rests there a moment, fondly, as though it were a medal.

4. Breck's chandlery

Read when they go in. The Gull sent them; Breck knows it before they say so.

Widow Breck's chandlery is a deep, dark shop near the top of Tarpot Lane that smells of tar, hemp, lamp oil and wax, so crowded with stock that you have to turn sideways to reach the counter: coils of rope to the ceiling, lanterns hung in strings, blocks and tackle, oakum, tallow, a barrel of belaying pins and a box of brass buttons for sailors who have lost theirs.

Behind the counter, under a lamp, a small sharp woman in widow's black and a leather apron is weighing out nails. She looks at you over her spectacles for exactly as long as it takes to decide who sent you, and smiles.

“Well,” she says. “You'll be wanting the good stock, then. Come through.”

The Gull sends them to @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActBreck000]{Widow Annis Breck} on Tarpot Lane, on her account, for whatever they need: thieves' tools, a dark lantern, a grapnel and fifty feet of silk line, a glazier's diamond, soft-soled shoes, and a builder's plan of the museum that Breck bought from a builder's widow years ago (it matches the scene exactly). Breck is helpful, quick, shrewd — and she asks one question too many: “And which night would that be, dear?”

The leak

Breck sold the Gull's face to the Weigher, and if the party tells her the night, she sells that too. Signs, for anyone paying attention:

  • Insight DC 13: she is frightened, not of them, and guilty about something.
  • Perception DC 15: a child's tin soldier on the shelf behind her, set apart from the stock and carefully dusted.
  • Following her after they leave (Stealth against passive Perception 14): she shuts the shop at once and walks straight to the weigh-house in Orgsworth.

What they can do about it:

  • Feed her the wrong night. The Weigher does not know the Gull has called the Low Table for the Day 15 tide — he means to call it himself, once he has the Pearl — so a later night suits him. His crew goes over the museum roof the night after the Kestrel Wife sails, and steals Pike's copy.
  • Turn her. Her grandson Kit owes the Weigher forty gold lions. Pay it at the weigh-house (the clerk hands over the marker), or bring her the Gull's word that Kit is safe, and she weeps, and tells the Weigher whatever night they like.
  • Tell the Gull. She deals with it quietly — Breck and Kit are on a fishing boat to Breck's sister up the coast by morning — and the Weigher learns nothing more.
  • Do nothing. The Weigher's crew comes over the museum roof on the same night as the party. See @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgNight00]{The Night}.

Read aloud — the weigh-house

If they go to the weigh-house in Orgsworth: following Breck, or to pay Kit's marker.

The city weigh-house stands among the Orgsworth warehouses like a chapel among barns: a tall, plain stone hall with great doors at both ends, so that a cart can drive in at one, stop on the scale and drive out at the other. The scale fills the middle of the floor, a beam as long as a ship's yard slung from the roof, with iron weights stacked beside it like loaves, and clerks at high desks along the walls writing everything down.

At the far end, in a fur-collared coat, a stout, mild-looking man is watching a bale of wool being weighed with the tender attention of a man watching his own child. Every clerk in the building knows exactly where he is standing.

That is @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActWeigh000]{the Weigher}. He does nothing in his own weigh-house. If they brawled with Dogger at the Mermaid's he has heard them described, and he is very polite; the clerk hands over Kit's marker for forty gold lions, and the Weigher watches them all the way out.

Optional: the front door

Read when they come to the Performers' Guild. Pippa is in the middle of a rehearsal.

The Performers' Guild is a theatre that has swallowed a guildhall: a stage door off a lane behind the Promenade, a corridor of costume rails, and beyond them the dark of an empty house with one lamp lit on the stage. On the stage a small woman in a borrowed chain of office and an enormous false belly is being the Lord Mayor of Gradsul to an audience of three stagehands, and the stagehands are crying with laughter.

She sees you in the wings, stops dead in the middle of a line, and takes off the belly.

“Strangers,” says Pippa Lark, delighted. “At this hour. Come and tell me a story — a good one — and then tell me what you want.”

For a party that would rather talk than climb: @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActLark0000]{Pippa Lark} at the Performers' Guild will dress them as Sea Mages come to renew the gallery ward — the wardens have never seen Lusk's face, and the Sea Mages do send people at the turn of the season — and coach them for an evening, in exchange for a good story. It need not be true, or theirs; it only needs to be good. Pike will forge the Sea Mages' warrant (he has their seal in his pattern book). See the approach on The Night.

The Royal Museum

@UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-scenes.Scene.BR2T1ScnMuse0000]{Gradsul — The Royal Museum}: both floors of one narrow townhouse (two floors over a cellar), side by side, street front at the bottom of both. Ground floor on the left, upper floor on the right; the two staircases are the same stair. Five-foot squares.

Ground floor (left)

  • Entrance hall. Double front doors to the street, barred inside at night. The Keeper's desk, a coat stand, the donation box on its post. Low in the street wall to the right of the doors, the coal-chute hatch.
  • The Wreck Room (left). A great crowned figurehead on trestles — hollow at the back, and a Small creature fits inside — two anchors, a ship's bell on a frame, a wheel, coils of old cable. Doors to the entrance hall and the stair hall; open at the back to the rear passage.
  • Stair hall (right). The stair rises toward the back of the house to the upper floor. Under it, at its foot by the outer wall, the narrow cellar stair behind a little arched door bolted on this side.
  • Wardens' room (back left). Two cots, a table with a lantern and a game of cards, a cold hearth, and the bell-rope, which rings a bell on the roof that the Watch House hears. The wardens' ward-token hangs on a nail by the door.
  • Keeper's office (back right). Papers, cabinets, a narrow cot, and in the desk drawer the Keeper's spare keys, the domed case's among them (Investigation DC 12 to find).
  • Rear passage and back yard. The back door opens on a walled yard with a rain barrel, a privy and a narrow gate in the far wall (locked, thieves' tools DC 12; the wall is 8 feet, Athletics DC 10).
  • The cellar (not drawn): the coal pile under the chute, packing crates of things the museum has never catalogued, and the stair up to the little arched door.

Upper floor (right)

  • The gallery. One long room with four tall windows on the street, two rows of glass-topped cases of ship models down a carpet runner, charts on the walls. Warded.
  • The alcove. Up two shallow steps at the back of the gallery, under a square skylight, the round glass-domed pedestal case with the Pearl in it, and small cases around the walls. Warded — the skylight is no way round it.
  • The stair head (right). The stair arrives at the back, under an archway and a second, smaller skylight, and opens into the gallery there. Not warded. The arch is the threshold.
  • The workroom (back right). A bench, tools, open crates and packing straw. Not warded — but its only door opens into the alcove, so anyone in here after lock-up is shut in until dawn unless they carry a token. A new crate arrived today.

The wardens

Two @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActWarden00]{Museum Night Wardens}, old marines, passive Perception 15. Hab Rowe walks the rounds with a lantern every half hour — entrance hall, Wreck Room, stair, gallery (with the token), back down — and the walk takes ten minutes. Sully Tate sits in the wardens' room by the bell-rope with the cards and does not leave it. They are kind, sixty, and not brave: each will pull the bell-rope long before he does anything heroic. Killing either is murder.

The Sea-Mages' ward

Laid by @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActLusk0000]{Sea-Mage Perrin Lusk} on the gallery and its alcove, from the moment the Keeper locks up until dawn:

  • Any creature of Tiny size or larger that enters the gallery, or moves any distance within it, rings a bell in the Sea Mages' hall across the city. Nothing happens here; nobody here hears it.
  • It counts creatures, not noise or light. Invisibility, silence and pass without trace do not help. Wild shape does not help: a cat is a creature. A familiar is a creature.
  • A creature carrying one of the three brass ward-tokens passes freely — the Keeper's, the wardens' and Lusk's own. One token, one creature.
  • Anyone already standing in the gallery when the ward wakes at lock-up rings it the first time they move. Hiding in the gallery at closing is the one place in the building not to hide.
  • Detect magic shows the whole room faintly glowing (abjuration). Dispel magic ends it — automatically with a slot of 4th level or higher, otherwise a DC 14 spellcasting check — quietly, but Lusk feels it go out.
  • When it rings, Lusk sends to the Watch House, and a Watch patrol reaches the museum ten minutes later.

The Pearl and the case

The domed case is locked: thieves' tools DC 15, or the Keeper's key from his desk. Inside, on a faded velvet cushion, the Mooncurser's Pearl: black, the size of a pigeon's egg, in a tarnished silver setting shaped like a gull's foot, three claws, on a short chain. Beside it a little card in the Keeper's hand. It is not magic. The swap takes one action and a steady hand (Sleight of Hand DC 10; anyone can do it with a minute and care), and the copy must sit exactly where the Pearl sat or Hab will notice on his next round (Perception against the swapper's Sleight of Hand).

Heat

Six segments. The job is Clean only if Heat never reaches 5.

MarkFor
1A failed Stealth check within earshot of a warden; glass cut or a latch forced; a door that is not quietly opened; any spell inside that a warden could see; a warden who notices something odd (his passive Perception beats the Stealth by less than 5).
2A warden who sees an intruder clearly; any fight inside the building, each round it lasts.
3The ward rings.
AtWhat happens
3Hab comes to look, lantern up, calling out. A cat, a draught, a fallen crate: Deception DC 12 from the dark and he goes back grumbling.
5Sully pulls the bell-rope. The roof bell rings, the Watch House hears it, and a patrol is at the front doors in ten rounds. The street wakes up. Gone before the patrol arrives, faces unseen: Noticed.
6Hue and cry: whistles, the Watch at front and back, and the Harbour Warden will hold the morning tide. See @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgPay0000]{Payoff & Consequences}.

The Night

Night of Day 14 on @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-scenes.Scene.BR2T1ScnMuse0000]{Gradsul — The Royal Museum}. Darkness is on and token vision is on; the lights are the wardens' lantern, a night lamp by the Keeper's desk, a street lamp at the door and the moon through both skylights. Hab Rowe's walking lantern is his own.

Read aloud — Havverd, after midnight

Read as they reach the museum's street, whatever the approach (for a stay-behind, read it to whoever is outside). Adjust the weather to the complication you chose.

Havverd sleeps early and sleeps well. The street outside the Royal Museum is empty from end to end: shuttered fronts, a cat on a step, one street lamp burning by the museum's barred front doors, and the moon coming and going behind thin cloud. Somewhere toward the harbour a watchman's whistle sounds, a long way off, and is answered.

The museum is dark except for a faint yellow glow at the back of the ground floor, where the wardens keep their lamp. As you watch, a second light moves slowly along the upstairs windows, from one end of the gallery to the other, and goes out of sight. Half an hour, then, before it comes round again.

Approaches

Stay behind

Go in as afternoon visitors and do not come out. The Keeper walks the building at closing and glances into every room (passive Perception 12; Stealth against it). The figurehead in the Wreck Room takes a Small creature. The cellar takes anyone, because the Keeper never goes down there — but he bolts its little door behind him, so somebody has to work the bolt from the stair-hall side or with a wire. Not the gallery — anyone in it when the ward wakes rings it the first time they move — and not the workroom, whose only door is in the warded alcove. The front doors are barred from inside, so a stay-behind can let the others in, quietly (Stealth DC 12, or 1 Heat).

Over the roof

Up from the lane behind the yard (Athletics DC 12 with the grapnel; the roofs are slate and steep). The stair-head skylight: latch, thieves' tools DC 13, or the glazier's diamond and a minute; forced, 1 Heat. It drops onto the stair head, outside the ward. The alcove skylight is easier to open and puts them inside the ward.

Through the cellar

The coal chute is two feet square. Elle fits; a Small wild shape fits; a Medium creature squeezes (Acrobatics DC 15, failure stuck and 1 Heat). The cellar is dark and black with coal dust. The little arched door at the top of the cellar stair is bolted on the stair-hall side: a thin wire through the gap (Sleight of Hand DC 13), or a Tiny creature — a familiar, a wild-shaped mouse — through the gap under it with a bit of string.

The front door, with a story

Dressed by Pippa Lark as Sea Mages come to renew the ward, with Pike's warrant. Deception against the wardens' Insight (+1); advantage if Pippa coached them. It works: Hab unbars the door and takes them up to the gallery arch himself, and there he hands the wardens' token to whichever Sea Mage looks most senior, as he has seen the apprentices do. One token, one creature: one of them can walk into the gallery and renew the ward, and the rest work from the arch while Hab watches. The swap has to happen under his nose — a distraction and Sleight of Hand DC 15, or a reason to send him downstairs — and the token goes back to him at the door. If the story fails, Hab bars the door again and shouts for Sully through it: 3 Heat, and the next mark brings Sully to the rope.

The Keeper's token

With a ward-token from the lecture or the nail, one creature walks into the gallery as though it owned it. It still needs the case opened and the wardens avoided.

Complications

Pick one, or roll a d6, or none if the plan is already hard enough.

d6Complication
1Fog off the harbour. Stealth outside has advantage; the Watch takes twice as long to arrive.
2The under-keeper, Neddy Marle, is asleep in the Keeper's office tonight after a quarrel with his wife. A light sleeper and the worst liar in Gradsul.
3The Keeper comes back at midnight for his lenses, knocks until Sully unbars the door, chats, and potters in the gallery for ten minutes with his token. If his token has been lifted, he finds out now: he goes pale, sends Sully for the Watch, and it is Heat 5.
4The new crate in the workroom holds a stuffed crocodile from the southern jungles, upright. Anyone moving in the workroom without care (Dexterity DC 12) knocks it over: 1 Heat.
5The watcher on the corner is awake, and whistles if he sees any face he knows — a Mooncurser's, or a PC who brawled with Dogger at the Mermaid's (Stealth against passive 13).
6Rain. Roofs slick (Athletics at disadvantage), but the noise on the slates gives Stealth inside advantage.

The Weigher's crew

If Breck sold the night and nobody stopped her, @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActDogger00]{Dogger Haines} and three @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActWTough00]{Weigher's Toughs} come over the roof an hour after midnight — or whenever the party is deepest into the job — and through the alcove skylight, because nobody told them about the ward. So they ring it: the Watch is ten minutes away from that moment, whatever the Heat.

When the Weigher's crew comes through the alcove skylight.

Glass breaks above the alcove — not loudly: one pane, knocked in with an elbow wrapped in sacking — and a rope comes down through the skylight into the moonlight, and then a man on the rope, and then another. Four of them, big men in dark smocks, landing heavily on the alcove steps beside the Pearl's case.

[If they fought Dogger at the Mermaid's:] The last one down is grinning. You have seen that grin before, across a room.

Nothing rings. Nothing flashes. Nothing happens at all.

  • They want the Pearl, not a fight. A fight in the gallery is 2 Heat a round.
  • If the swap is already done, the best move in the building is to get out and let them take the copy and run straight into the Watch with it. A ring the party did not cause does not count against them: if they were clear and unseen when the patrol arrived, the outcome is Noticed, no tide is held because the Watch has its thieves, and the Gull will be delighted for a year.
  • If it is not, it is a race to the case, or a deal (Dogger is reasonable, for a price), or a fight the Watch will finish.

If it goes loud

When Sully pulls the bell-rope (Heat 5).

Up on the roof a bell begins to ring: not a church bell but a hard, flat, iron clang, over and over, the way a bell rings when a frightened man is hauling on its rope with both hands. All down the street, shutters bang open. A dog starts up. Lamps come on in the windows one after another, and somewhere toward Gartten, far off but already answering, a whistle shrills, and then another.

The fallback is a fight and a run, and the run is better.

  • Inside: the two wardens, then a @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActWatch000]{Watch} patrol of four with a sergeant at the front doors (ten rounds after the bell), then another at the yard gate two minutes later. They take prisoners.
  • The run: roofs, yard or lane, to the river stair under the castle hill, where a Mooncurser boat waits if the Gull conceded one. Three checks of the party's choice (Athletics, Acrobatics, Stealth, a clever spell); two successes and they are on the water.
  • The line: killing a warden, a watchman or the Keeper turns every outcome to Blood. Say so before anyone swings, if the table looks like forgetting.

Payoff & Consequences

Before dawn on Day 15, the net loft. Then the morning tide.

The handover

Before dawn on Day 15, in the net loft, if they bring her the Pearl. As Pike hands over the papers, show @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgHandout]{Pike's Papers}, or @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GullJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GuPgTicket0]{The Weigh-Ticket} if there is no docket (see below). If the morning tide is held, the walk to the quay happens that evening instead.

The Gull takes the Pearl in her bare hand and holds it to the lamp for a long moment, turning it, saying nothing. It is only a black pearl in a tarnished silver claw. For that moment her face is the face of a girl of twelve.

Then she puts it on its chain round her neck, under the grey silk, and is herself again.

Pike, beside her, hands over a waxed-cloth wallet tied with tarred twine, with a small bow to each of you in turn.

She walks with you as far as the end of the quay in her veil and her grey gown, her coachman a step behind — a poor relation seeing off some acquaintances — and turns back before the Kestrel Wife's plank without a word. As the bell at the Foaming Tower rings you out, somewhere under the Docklands, people you will never meet are sitting down at a table.

They sail with the Kestrel Wife — on the evening tide, if the morning one was held — with nothing. No milestone.

If the samples survived the Ford, or nobody told the Gull they were lost, there is no docket: Pike makes only the weigh-ticket, and the handout to show is Handout — The Weigh-Ticket.

What the papers do in Hardby

  • The docket (only if the samples were lost at the Ford): the letters and the bales agree on paper. The first crack in the cover from @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1FordJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1FdPgTerr000]{Terrain, the Cart Clock & Outcomes} is closed.
  • The weigh-ticket: the customs boy who boards at the mole takes it and the coin in it, counts bales, and writes nothing down, whatever happened to the hull. If the hull track reached segment 2, the one-flicker line in @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1QRefJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1QrPgHandoff]{Hand-off to Phase 3} does not happen. If it did not, nothing changes.

Write it on the back of the hand-off sheet now: Gull's papers — docket (y/n), weigh-ticket (y/n).

If they double-cross her

Keep the Pearl, sell it, or hand it to the Weigher, and the Gull settles it herself, on her own waterfront, before they sail: no papers, a very cold morning on the quay, and every Mooncurser in the Docklands knowing their faces for as long as they live. She tells nobody outside Gradsul anything; she has nobody there to tell. A Gradsul fence will not touch the Pearl at any price, and nobody else on the coast knows what it is.

If they never take the job

She thanks them for the Mermaid's, sends a basket of oranges and a bottle of good Keoish wine to their wool-house, and they never hear of her again. The Weigher has bigger concerns than five strangers who leave in three days.

One last thing

If they did the job: the first night out, when they go below.

Below decks, in the dry dark among the bales, something pale is tucked into the lashings of your own: a single feather, grey and white. A gull's. Nobody aboard saw who put it there, and when you ask, nobody aboard has the least idea what you mean.

Pike's Papers

Two documents in a waxed-cloth wallet, tied with tarred twine.

A docket of provenance on a Gradsul wool-house's good paper, under its seal: that the samples carried by the delegation were spoiled in the wet on the road to Gradsul and were replaced at the house's own warehouse in Orgsworth, by its factor, from the same clip, and that the house warrants them. Signed by the factor, witnessed by his clerk. The ink is a week old. It was written last night.

A weigh-ticket from the city weigh-house of Gradsul for the delegation's bales, with the Deputy Weighmaster's stamp, and across the bottom in a neat clerk's hand: weighed short. Folded inside it, a single gold lion.

Clipped to the ticket, a strip of paper in a different, careful hand:

Give this to whoever comes aboard at the mole. Say nothing else. — P.
